questions.prompt: Which branch of quantum computing research is most realistically open to a self-taught software engineer without a physics PhD or lab access?
options: Applied/software research — building tooling, running benchmarks, and implementing algorithm variants on cloud-accessible hardware
Experimental/hardware research — building and characterizing physical qubits in a physics lab
Theoretical research — proving new complexity bounds and designing new error-correcting codes
None of the branches are realistically open without a PhD
questions.explain: Applied/software research runs on cloud-accessible hardware and simulators and depends on software skill rather than lab access or deep theoretical-physics training, making it the realistic entry point for a non-PhD software engineer.

questions.prompt: Select every property this course requires of a usable research hypothesis.
options: Testable — some experiment could produce measurable support or contradiction
Falsifiable — some possible outcome could show it's wrong
Guaranteed to be confirmed by the experiment that tests it
Named with a specific comparison/baseline condition
Published in a peer-reviewed journal before the experiment begins
questions.explain: A usable hypothesis must be testable and falsifiable, and must name a specific comparison condition (without one, claims like 'improves results' have nothing concrete to measure against). It must NOT be guaranteed to be confirmed — that would make it unfalsifiable — and prior publication is not a requirement.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: on real quantum hardware, a single circuit execution is called one ________, and because measurement is inherently probabilistic, many of these are needed to build a trustworthy probability distribution.
questions.explain: A shot is one repeated execution of a quantum circuit. Reporting a result from a single shot is like judging a coin's fairness from one flip — hundreds to thousands of shots are standard practice to build a measured distribution with quantifiable uncertainty.

questions.prompt: A student runs their novel error-mitigation technique once on cloud hardware this week and compares it to a baseline number quoted from a paper published two years ago on a different device. What is the strongest objection to this comparison?
options: Too many variables differ at once — hardware, calibration window, and time — so it is not a controlled comparison
Comparing to any published number is always invalid under any circumstances
Zero-noise extrapolation cannot be benchmarked against a baseline in principle
The comparison is valid as long as both numbers are positive
questions.explain: Real quantum hardware drifts over time due to recalibration and usage. Comparing results from different hardware, at different times, with different calibration states confounds multiple variables at once, which is why interleaved, same-device, same-window comparisons are the standard this course teaches.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about reproducibility, replicability, and robustness, as distinguished in this course.
options: Reproducibility uses the original code and data to get the same result
Replicability uses an independent implementation of the same method to get a consistent result
Robustness tests whether a result holds under reasonable variations like a different seed or device
A result can pass reproducibility while failing replicability, pointing to a bug or hidden assumption in the original code
These three terms are fully interchangeable and always test the exact same thing
questions.explain: These are three genuinely distinct goals. A reproducibility pass and a replicability pass can disagree, which is itself informative — it points to something specific (often a bug or hidden assumption) rather than meaning the terms are interchangeable.

questions.prompt: Why does the course describe quantum hardware as adding a reproducibility challenge that classical software research doesn't face?
options: The hardware itself is not a fixed instrument — its noise characteristics genuinely change over time due to drift and recalibration
Quantum circuits cannot be written down precisely enough to ever be reproduced
Classical software never has any reproducibility challenges of its own
Quantum hardware providers deliberately randomize all results to prevent reproduction
questions.explain: Classical reproducibility assumes a nominally stable computing environment. Quantum hardware breaks this assumption because the physical device's noise characteristics genuinely drift over time, making an exact-match reproduction attempt partially a robustness check whether intended or not.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: before concluding that a published paper's claim doesn't hold, you must first rule out the far more common explanation — a bug or ________ in your own implementation.
questions.explain: The course's diagnostic checklist places implementation bugs and parameter mismatches first, precisely because they are the most common sources of discrepancy — escalating to 'the paper is wrong' without ruling these out first is a real research-integrity failure mode.

questions.prompt: A paper reports a 0.18 error reduction with a stated uncertainty of ±0.02. A student's independent replication measures a 0.155 reduction. What does this course's framework say about this result?
options: 0.155 falls outside the paper's 0.16–0.20 range, suggesting a real discrepancy worth further diagnosis, not an automatic confirmation or refutation
0.155 falls comfortably inside the paper's range, confirming an exact match
The comparison is meaningless because replication attempts can never be compared numerically
This automatically proves the original paper's claim is fraudulent
questions.explain: 0.18 ± 0.02 gives a range of 0.16–0.20; 0.155 falls below that range. Per the course's diagnostic checklist, this is a real discrepancy worth further diagnosis — not grounds for either an automatic confirmation or an accusation of fraud.

questions.prompt: Select every project type this course names as a realistic capstone shape.
options: Reproduction + extension of a specific, modest published result
A comparative benchmark of two or three techniques on a fixed circuit and device
Applied algorithm implementation and rigorous characterization of its behavior
Inventing an entirely new quantum algorithm with no prior basis
Proving a new theorem about quantum complexity classes
questions.explain: The three realistic capstone shapes are reproduction + extension, comparative benchmark, and applied algorithm implementation/characterization. Inventing new algorithms or proving new theorems is explicitly set at the graduate-research level, above a course capstone's bar.

questions.prompt: Why does this course describe 'reproduction + extension' as often the strongest capstone shape for a learner at this stage?
options: The reproduction half gives a known target to validate your own competence against before adding an original extension, making the project self-correcting
It requires no understanding of the original paper at all
It is the only capstone shape the course permits
It is guaranteed to produce a publishable result
questions.explain: If a reproduction attempt doesn't track the original paper reasonably well, that catches a methodology problem before an extension is built on a shaky foundation — this is what makes the shape self-correcting, not a guarantee of publication.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a pre-committed, ordered list of which parts of a capstone proposal to drop first if time runs short is called a ________.
questions.explain: The cut list is decided before building begins, while not under time pressure, so a schedule slip becomes 'execute step 1 of the plan' rather than an improvised scramble.

questions.prompt: Select every time-cost category this course says is easy to underestimate in a quantum computing capstone.
options: Queue time on shared cloud quantum hardware, separate from actual run time
Iteration count — realistic projects often need two or three build-run-analyze passes, not one
Write-up and presentation time, which deserves as much calendar time as the experimental work
The time needed to read the course's own lesson guides
The time needed to format a resume bullet
questions.explain: The course specifically names queue time, iteration count, and write-up/presentation time as the three categories most often underestimated — not time spent reading course material or resume formatting, which are comparatively small and don't scale with experimental complexity.

questions.prompt: Why does this course recommend validating analysis code (like a zero-noise-extrapolation fit) on a simulator with an INJECTED, known noise model, rather than only a noiseless simulator?
options: A known injected model lets you compute the true answer yourself in advance and check whether your analysis code recovers it, before trusting it on real hardware's unknown noise
Injected noise models always run faster than noiseless simulators
A noiseless simulator cannot execute circuits with more than one qubit
Real hardware and injected noise models always produce numerically identical results
questions.explain: A noiseless simulator has no noise for mitigation/extrapolation logic to act on, so it can't validate that logic at all. An injected, known noise model provides a ground truth you control, letting you confirm the analysis code actually works before applying it to real, unknown hardware noise.

questions.prompt: Select every piece of metadata this course says should be recorded for each real-hardware run, at the time it executes.
options: The exact device name and calibration/backend-properties timestamp
The exact shot count and circuit identifier
Timestamps for when the job was submitted versus when it actually executed
The researcher's personal mood that day
A path or link to the raw result data
questions.explain: The course's run log format requires device, calibration timestamp, shot count, circuit identifier, submission/execution timestamps, and a data path — all captured as-you-go because device states can't be reliably reconstructed afterward. Personal mood is not relevant experimental metadata.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the dishonest practice of rewriting a hypothesis after seeing experimental results, to match whatever was actually found, is known in research methodology as ________.
acceptedAnswers: Hypothesizing After the Results are Known
questions.explain: HARKing (Hypothesizing After the Results are Known) is the specific failure mode this course warns against. The structural fix is referring back to a dated, written proposal that recorded the original prediction before the data was seen.

questions.prompt: A capstone's initial, non-interleaved 3- vs 5-qubit comparison showed an unexpected pattern that was traced to a six-hour calibration gap between runs. After a same-window interleaved retry reversed the pattern back to what the hypothesis predicted, what does this course say should happen to the data from the ORIGINAL run?
options: It should be kept and reported alongside the corrected result, since the discrepancy between them is itself part of the finding
It should be deleted immediately since it was wrong
It should be hidden from the final report to avoid looking unprofessional
It should replace the corrected result as the only number reported
questions.explain: The course explicitly recommends keeping both the original and corrected results, since reporting both demonstrates real diagnostic work — identifying and controlling for a confound — rather than just presenting a different number with no explanation.

questions.prompt: Select every condition this course says makes a capstone re-run worth doing.
options: It targets one specific, identified, fixable confound
It fits inside the remaining time budget, including its own queue time
It would meaningfully change what can be honestly concluded
It adds an entirely new, previously unplanned comparison condition
It is requested by the hardware provider's support team
questions.explain: A worthwhile re-run is targeted, fits the time budget, and would change the honest conclusion. Adding unplanned new scope is the scope-creep pattern the course warns against, not a justification for re-running.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the 'experiment summary' document this course asks you to write at finalization time?
options: A short working document extracting and organizing key facts (hypothesis, runs, findings, uncertainties) to make the full report faster to write
The final report itself, submitted instead of the full methods/results/limitations/conclusions report
A public announcement posted before any data analysis is complete
A legal disclaimer required before using any quantum cloud hardware
questions.explain: The experiment summary is explicitly described as a bridging document, not the final report — it pre-organizes key facts so the formal write-up (methods, results, limitations, conclusions) is faster and more accurate to produce.

questions.prompt: Select every element this course says belongs in a capstone's Limitations section.
options: Any confound identified during the project, such as a calibration-window gap
Specification choices you made yourself where the methodology was ambiguous
Scope boundaries you deliberately didn't cover, such as untested qubit counts
A single apologetic sentence with no real detail, placed at the very end
Adjectives describing how well the experiment went, with no specific numbers
questions.explain: A strong limitations section names real confounds, documented specification choices, and explicit scope boundaries — not a thin, apologetic one-liner or vague adjectives, both of which the course flags as red flags of an overstated report.

questions.prompt: Why does this course say a technical presentation's structure should differ from the written report's structure, even when covering the same capstone?
options: A presentation is linear and time-boxed, so it should lead with the question and headline finding rather than building up to a conclusion the way a report can
Because presentations are not allowed to include any numerical results
Because written reports are always shorter than presentations
Because technical audiences never ask follow-up questions
questions.explain: A report can be read at the reader's own pace and skipped around in; a time-boxed presentation needs to lead with the question and finding, supporting it afterward, rather than the report's methods-first build-up.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: translating a technical result for a non-specialist audience means replacing jargon with accurate, accessible language — the goal is NOT to remove detail, but to ________ the framing without losing accuracy.
questions.explain: The course is explicit that removing detail isn't the goal — replacing precise-but-opaque technical language with precise-but-accessible plain language is, preserving the same underlying meaning and scope limits.

questions.prompt: Select every item this course says a portfolio-ready capstone repository needs, beyond the raw code.
options: A README with an orienting summary: the question, the finding, and the repo's organization
The written report as a standalone, readable document
Both the technical and general-audience presentation slides
The final dataset and run log in a plain, inspectable format
A guarantee from the author that the hypothesis was fully confirmed
questions.explain: The course lists an orienting README, a readable report, both presentation versions, and an inspectable final dataset/run log as what makes a repository portfolio-ready — not a guarantee of a confirmed hypothesis, which would misrepresent partially-supported or unexpected results.

questions.prompt: A reviewer comments that your conclusion claims a result is 'significant' but no significance test appears anywhere in your results section. Per this course's feedback-triage framework, how should this be handled?
options: As a must-fix — either add the significance test or remove the unsupported claim so the conclusion matches what the results actually show
As a stylistic preference to note and ignore
As feedback that should be dismissed because reviewers can't comment on statistical language
As an issue to address only if time allows after the report is already finalized
questions.explain: This is a genuine unsupported claim — the conclusion asserts something the results section doesn't demonstrate — exactly what the course's must-fix triage category is meant to catch before a report is considered final.

questions.prompt: According to this course, which roles are realistic destinations for a strong portfolio built through this entire 14-course path?
options: Quantum Software Developer and Quantum Algorithms Engineer
Quantum Research Engineer in a hardware lab, with no further study required
Senior quantum research scientist at a national lab immediately after graduation
Any quantum-related role regardless of its stated qualifications
questions.explain: The course names Quantum Software Developer and Quantum Algorithms Engineer as realistic destinations, while stating plainly that Quantum Research Engineer and hardware-lab or senior research-scientist roles typically require graduate-level qualifications this path alone does not replace.

questions.prompt: Select every consequence this course names of quantum computing being 'a small, early, fast-changing field.'
options: Fewer open roles at any given time compared to mainstream software engineering
Less standardized, less repeatable hiring processes at many companies
A market that shifts as companies' funding and technical strategy change
Complete absence of any real jobs in the field
No need to build a specific, strong portfolio since credentials alone suffice
questions.explain: The course names fewer open roles, less standardized hiring, and strategic shifts as real consequences — and explicitly uses these to argue FOR building a strong, specific portfolio, not that no real jobs exist or that credentials alone are sufficient.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: because no single industry-standard certification governs quantum computing hiring, this course teaches that real, verifiable ________ work functions as the actual credential that matters.
questions.explain: With no dominant standardized credential like CompTIA or AWS certifications, hiring in this field leans on direct evidence of capability — real project and portfolio work, especially a reproduced research experiment.

questions.prompt: What does this course say graduate study adds that this path, by design, does not provide?
options: Hands-on physical lab experience and mentored, multi-year original research under a PI's guidance
Fluency in Qiskit and Q#, which graduate study teaches for the first time
Basic linear algebra, which this path never actually covered
Knowledge of the landmark quantum algorithms, absent from this path entirely
questions.explain: The course names physical lab access and mentored, multi-year original research as the structural gaps graduate study fills — not fundamentals like linear algebra, toolchain fluency, or the landmark algorithms, all of which this path already covers.

questions.prompt: Select every statement this course makes about alternatives to a full PhD for research-adjacent quantum computing work.
options: A master's degree alone can open some research-engineer and applied-research roles that don't require independent research leadership
Research-engineer roles supporting PhD researchers' tooling and benchmarking needs are reachable with this path's foundation plus continued project work
The Quantum Software Developer / Algorithms Engineer tier is a real, different destination, not a lesser consolation prize
There are no realistic alternatives to a full PhD in this field whatsoever
A full PhD is required for every single role this path's graduates could ever pursue
questions.explain: The course explicitly describes a master's degree, research-engineer roles, and the Software Developer/Algorithms Engineer tier as real, reachable alternatives short of a full PhD — directly contradicting the idea that no alternatives exist or that a PhD is universally required.

questions.prompt: Why does this course recommend including the confound-and-correction story from your capstone when answering 'walk me through a project' in an interview, rather than only describing the clean final result?
options: Interviewers who have done real research themselves tend to find candidates who honestly describe handling an unexpected result MORE credible than those who report only clean successes
Because interviewers always prefer the longest possible answer regardless of content
Because omitting any part of a project is considered fraud under interview law
Because clean successes are never believed by any interviewer under any circumstances
questions.explain: The course states that a candidate who reports only a flawless result on a first real research-style project often reads as LESS credible, not more, to an interviewer with real research experience — the honest confound story is a stronger signal of genuine capability.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: when asked a technical interview question you genuinely don't know the answer to, this course recommends saying so plainly, then ________ toward a partial answer from what you do know, rather than guessing confidently.
questions.explain: Honest acknowledgment followed by visible reasoning from related knowledge demonstrates real analytical ability — usually what's actually being tested — rather than confident guessing that risks being wrong and unconvincing.
